newsitem.title: CANADA: Space-ground U.S. telecope combo glimpses galaxies.
newsitem.headline: Space-ground U.S. telecope combo glimpses galaxies.

text.p: The orbiting Hubble Space Telescope has been teamed with a massive telescope based in Hawaii to give a glimpse at distant galaxies even before most of their stars were born, researchers reported on Thursday.

"There's certainly this hint that we've seen over the edge, that we've seen essentially beyond the epoch where most of the galaxies were forming most of their stars," Henry Ferguson of the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore said at a news conference.

Astronomers have long searched for an epoch of galaxy formation, but this was the first time a team of scientists was been able to peer back before that era -- which may have occurred when the universe was perhaps one-fifth its current age -- to a time when very few stars were being formed, Ferguson said.
To reach this point, astronomers used the Hubble's Deep Field view of the cosmos, which gave a narrow but very probing vision of the universe that essentially allowed scientists to look back in time.

Beginning with this narrow view of the sky, astronomers used the Hawaii-based Keck telescope to study 24 of the faint, blobby-looking galaxies in detail, researchers said on the closing day of a meeting of the American Astronomical Society in Toronto.

They found that the many distant objects in the Hubble image could not have all developed into the kind of massive galaxies, like the Milky Way, which now exist. Instead these early objects may have merged to form today's large galaxies.

These early galaxies were at least as bright as the Milky Way, but only about one-tenth its size, and created stars at a much slower pace than the prolific galaxies of several billion years later, the scientists said.

The young stars' atmospheres showed signs of carbon, oxygen, silicon and other metals, which indicated generations of stars had come and gone even in these early days of the universe, possibly 2 billion years after the big bang.

Because the last two years sparked a keen debate over the age of the oldest stars -- some researchers theorised the earliest stars were older than the universe itself -- Ferguson used an earthly metaphor when asked what light these findings might shed on the age of the universe.

"It's like being on a boat in a lake and trying to determine the depth of the lake by counting the fish," Ferguson said. "... We really have to start understanding the fish before you can figure out the depth of the lake. We still don't understand the fish, but we're getting there."

In other research on galaxies presented on Thursday, scientists said they found new clues to mysterious phenomena known as gamma-ray bursts: huge, intense energy flashes that occur perhaps once or twice every day.

First identified by military satellites in the 1960s, gamma-ray bursts were long thought to occur within the Milky Way, but the latest research indicated strongly that these powerful explosions occurred outside our galaxy, the researchers said.
